qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Antoni Comín i Oliveres (NI), Carles Puigdemont i Casamajó (NI) Subject:

On 26 February 2024, the Spanish national newspaper El País published an article1 stating that the EU Intelligence and Situation Centre (EU INTCEN) had produced an intelligence report alleging Russian involvement in supporting the Catalan independence movement. This report was said to have been drafted in November 2017. In September 2021, The New York Times also referred to a report that may have been produced by EU INTCEN. However, in response to our inquiry E-004166/20212, the EEAS informed us that ‘EU INTCEN intelligence assessments are mainly based on the strategic intelligence assessments of EU Member States’ and that EU INTCEN was ‘not the author of the report mentioned in the article’. On 6 February 2024, Commission Vice-President Schinas stated in Parliament that there were reports of frequent and close contacts between Russian officials and representatives of a Catalan secessionist group between 2017 and 2020. We raised question P-000419/20243 regarding this issue, which has still not been answered. 1.
Did EU INTCEN draft the report mentioned in El País?
If so, did EU INTCEN produce the report on its own initiative, or upon the request of the VP/HR or another EU institution?
Is the report mentioned in El País the same one as that mentioned in The New York Times?
at: (English version) Priority question for written answer P-000419/24 to the Commission Carles Puigdemont i Casamajó (NI), Antoni Comín i Oliveres (NI) (7 February 2024) Subject: Grave accusations made by Commission Vice-President Schinas On Tuesday 6 February 2024, at Parliament’s plenary session in Strasbourg, Commission Vice-President Margaritis Schinas said that there were ‘reports on close and regular contacts, including organised visits, between Russian officials and representatives of a group of Catalan secessionists, in Spain, between 2017 and 2020 ’ (1). In December 2021, the European External Action Service responded to Written Question E-004166/2021 (2), saying that the EU Intelligence and Situation Centre (INTCEN) was ‘not the author of the intelligence report mentioned in the New York Times article’ and that the ‘EU INTCEN does not know who authored the report in question’ (3). The allegations of this Russian connection with Catalonia have been brought up for political reasons by some Spanish Members of the European Parliament. Vice-President Schinas has very close relations with the Spanish People’s Party (4). 1.
Did the EU INTCEN write one or several of the reports mentioned by Vice-President Schinas?
If not, what are Vice-President Schinas’s sources?

to the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Antoni Comín i Oliveres (NI), Carles Puigdemont i Casamajó (NI) (27 February 2024) Subject: Another newspaper article referring to a purported EU INTCEN intelligence report alleging links between Russia and the Catalan independence movement On 26 February 2024, the Spanish national newspaper El País published an article (5) stating that the EU Intelligence and Situation Centre (EU INTCEN) had produced an intelligence report alleging Russian involvement in supporting the Catalan independence movement. This report was said to have been drafted in November 2017. In September 2021, The New York Times also referred to a report that may have been produced by EU INTCEN. However, in response to our inquiry E-004166/2021 (6), the EEAS informed us that ‘EU INTCEN intelligence assessments are mainly based on the strategic intelligence assessments of EU Member States’ and that EU INTCEN was ‘not the author of the report mentioned in the article’. Did EU INTCEN draft the report mentioned in El País?

Joint answer given by High Representative/Vice-President Borrell i Fontelles on behalf of the European Commission (26 June 2024) The EU is alert to hybrid actions conducted or induced by the Russian Federation, which target the EU and its Member States. Concretely, revelations of Russian interference into European democratic processes are nothing new, but they remain deeply concerning and therefore the EU needs to keep vigilant. |(⸱1|)∙ |(⸱2|)∙ |(⸱3|)∙ |(⸱4|)∙ |(⸱5|)∙ |(⸱6|)∙ |(⸱7|)∙

Vice-President for ‘Promoting our European Way of Life’ in his plenary intervention of 6 February 2024 drew attention to the available sources that state this evidence, including Parliament resolutions. In its resolutions of 9 March 2022 (8) and 13 July 2023 (9), the Parliament asked for in-depth investigation of ‘findings about the close and regular contacts between Russian officials and representatives of a group of Catalan secessionists in Spain’ […]’ calling them ‘part of Russia’s wider strategy to use each and every opportunity to manipulate discourse in order to promote destabilisation’. The Parliament also expressed ‘concerns about Russia’s connections with several political parties and politicians in the EU and its wide-ranging interference with secessionist movements in European territories and in the EU, such as in Catalonia’ in its resolution of 1 June 2023 (10). The issue is also addressed in the Parliament’s most recent resolution of 8 February 2024 (11), which refers to numerous reports highlighting contacts and close personal relationships between secessionists in Catalonia, including authorities of the government of the autonomous community of Catalonia and the Kremlin, and expresses extreme concerns about these allegations. The EU Intelligence and Situation Centre (EU INTCEN) provides strategic intelligence on early warning, situational awareness, strategic foresight and threat assessments to support the various EU decision-making bodies. EU INTCEN intelligence assessments are mainly based on the strategic intelligence assessments of Member States’ intelligence and security services. The Commission does not have any comments on reports mentioned in the press.
